summary:
Maluku stands under Indonesia's national framework. Both sources audited for this province are national in scope, and neither records a Maluku-specific ordinance, police operation, protection scheme or service, so the assessment rests on the national picture those sources document.

The penal code signed on 6 December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and criminalises sexual activity between adults outside marriage. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of two years' imprisonment, while the national overview gives up to one year where an immediate family member lodges the complaint. Because Indonesia does not permit same-sex marriage, every sexual act by a same-sex couple falls within the outside-marriage offence. Reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Criminalisation below the national level exists in two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, which penalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. Two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in Aceh in February 2025. Maluku has no equivalent provincial provision.

Physical risk is rising across Indonesia. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism, placing them inside national defence policy.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians electronic ID cards, operating in nine provinces, as the document route. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution is silent on both.

On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected, by five votes to four, a petition to criminalise homosexuality. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, and a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage.
tangentialFactors:
Maluku's position differs from Aceh, where Sharia-based criminalisation produces punishments that apply to visitors present in that province; a traveller moving between provinces therefore faces materially different legal exposure under the same national flag.

The October 2025 presidential decree classifying LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat sits alongside the August 2026 reporting on vigilante mob attacks, indicating that official rhetoric and street-level violence are moving in the same direction rather than offsetting each other.

The 2023 Pew Research finding that 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage, together with Indonesia's vote against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, indicates the depth of social and diplomatic hostility a visibly gender-nonconforming visitor may encounter beyond formal legal provisions.
localsOnly:
Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach programme issuing electronic ID cards to transgender Indonesians, operating in nine provinces, as the practical document route; the standard legal gender recognition process still requires sex reassignment surgery plus judicial approval.

The Constitutional Court's 5-4 rejection on 14 December 2017 of a petition to criminalise homosexuality means the outside-marriage provision of the 2022 penal code, effective 2 January 2026, is the operative national instrument rather than a dedicated anti-sodomy statute.

National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections, and the Constitution is silent on sexual orientation and gender identity, leaving residents without a statutory remedy for harassment on these grounds.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Maluku-specific ordinance, police operation, protection scheme or service is recorded in the sources audited; whether the province has any undocumented local practice on these questions remains unresolved and is not sourced here.

The two national sources give different maximum penalties for the outside-marriage offence, two years in the Human Dignity Trust profile against one year where an immediate family member complains in the national overview; the reconciliation of these figures is unresolved in the inventory.

The status of the 2025 bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour, whether it has been enacted or remains under discussion, is unresolved in the sources.
